overview: This two-page register lists papers filed in 1941 concerning Japanese restrictions on the use of English and other foreign languages in telephone communications within the Japanese Empire. It traces exchanges between the U.S. Department of State and Ambassador Joseph C. Grew’s embassy from July through September 1941: notification of new Japanese regulations, consideration and authorization of a formal American protest, Japanese explanations invoking similar British regulations, U.S. insistence that diplomatic and consular communications required this facility, and the eventual announcement that foreign-language telephone conversations would again be permitted beginning September 13.

subfiles.title: List of papers on Japanese telephone laws and regulations
subfiles.about: A two-page file register summarizes diplomatic correspondence about Japan’s 1941 prohibition and subsequent restoration of foreign-language telephone communications.
subfiles.summary: The register records telegrams exchanged between the Department of State and the U.S. Embassy in Japan from July through September 1941. After new regulations prohibited English-language telephone conversations, the Department authorized a formal protest, although Grew warned that such a protest would probably be futile. Japanese officials attributed the measure to comparable British regulations, but Washington rejected that justification and pressed for a formal answer because telephone access was essential to American diplomatic and consular work. A September 19 telegram reported that the Japanese Foreign Office had permitted telephone conversations in foreign languages again as of the evening of September 13; the list also notes an August 19 report numbered 5795 on the restrictions.

interest: The register supplies a compact chronology of a small but revealing communications dispute during the deterioration of U.S.-Japanese relations in 1941. It shows how a seemingly technical language rule affected the daily functioning of diplomatic and consular offices and became the subject of a formal protest. Particularly useful are Grew’s assessment that protest would be futile, Japan’s appeal to British precedent, Washington’s rejection of that comparison, and the precise date on which foreign-language telephone conversations were restored.
